Click a day to load it on the map. Same jobs, same technicians, same distance rules.

How it works

  • Routes: every Tyre Fitting Request visit with a recorded actual start, done by the technicians based in London North East, Harlow, Chelmsford or Colchester.
  • What happened: each technician's visits in the order of their actual start times.
  • Start point: where each technician's first job of the day usually is, because some roster base centres are far from where the work starts.
  • Distance and time: straight line between postcodes × 1.3 for roads, at 30 km/h plus each job's planned duration. Gaps between jobs in the data work out at about 25 to 38 km/h.
  • Alternatives: keep every job, start from 07:30, aim to arrive within the booked slot, finish no later than the technician did, and stay within a usual van load of tyres. Solved with Google OR-Tools.
  • Postcode areas: statistics use all 54,921 Tyre Fitting Request appointments in the files, from every technician. Rates are hidden for districts with fewer than 20 appointments.

What it can't tell you

  • Real road distances, traffic, or where tyres are collected. The tyre and stock check is shown, not modelled.
  • Shift patterns, breaks, skills or van stock. Planners know things this data doesn't.
  • Same day changes. Planners route jobs as they arrive; this sees the whole day at once, so savings are an upper estimate.
  • Whether a saving would happen in practice. It's a reason to test with planners, not a result.
  • Headcount. A plan that leaves a technician free isn't a saving, because availability and other areas' demand aren't in the data.
  • Exact boundaries. District shapes come from Wikipedia's postcode maps; the roster and territory map have no effective dates.

With thanks to Mathew Taylor and the team at Kwik Fit, whose conversation at interview inspired this prototype. Built by Daniel Christopher on the assessment sample data. Not a Kwik Fit product.
